claims.text: Applying uniaxial bending strain to sputtered Nb-Ta-V-Mo-W high-entropy alloy films modifies interatomic distances.
Strain-induced changes in interatomic distances alter the electronic density of states near the Fermi level.
Changes in atomic spacing modify the electronic band structure of the alloy.
Strain-induced electronic-structure changes modify electron–phonon coupling strength.
Modification of electron–phonon coupling by strain causes a systematic change in superconducting critical temperature.
An increase in the density of states at the Fermi level will produce a higher critical temperature than in the unstrained film.
A decrease in the density of states at the Fermi level will produce a lower critical temperature than in the unstrained film.
Low-temperature scanning tunneling spectroscopy can assess strain-induced changes in the local electronic density of states.
Intrinsic chemical disorder can compete with or obscure strain-induced changes in superconducting behavior.
The proposed mechanism becomes influential only when strain-induced changes in interatomic distances are large enough to overcome intrinsic chemical-disorder effects.
The proposed mechanism applies primarily to controlled thin-film geometries.
The proposed mechanism may not extend to bulk-cast or heavily polycrystalline materials.
